theory.intro: A **minimum spanning tree (MST)** connects all $n$ vertices of a weighted graph using $n - 1$ edges with the lowest possible total weight. **Prim's algorithm** builds an MST by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge from any connected vertex to an unvisited vertex.
facts: A **minimum spanning tree (MST)** connects all $n$ vertices of a weighted network using $n - 1$ edges of lowest total weight.
**Prim's algorithm** can start at any vertex and always produces an MST with the same minimum total weight.
At each step of Prim's algorithm, check edges connected to all visited vertices, not just the latest vertex.
Never choose an edge that creates a **cycle** by reconnecting two vertices already in the tree.
Ties between equal lowest-weight edges can be chosen in any order without changing the total MST weight.
The total weight of an MST is the sum of its $n - 1$ edge weights.
steps: Choose the lowest-weight edge connected to the starting vertex
From all vertices currently in the tree, repeatedly add the lowest-weight edge to an unvisited vertex
Continue until all $n$ vertices are connected and sum the $n - 1$ edge weights

foundation.question_text:
While executing Prim's algorithm on a weighted network, the vertices currently in the tree are $\{A, B\}$.
The available edges connecting tree vertices to unvisited vertices are $AC=5, AD=3, BC=4, BD=6$.
State which edge is selected next and justify your choice.
foundation.solution_text:
$\text{Lowest weight} = \min(5, 3, 4, 6)$
$= 3$
Edge $AD$ is selected next because it has the lowest weight ($3$) connecting the current tree to an unvisited vertex.

foundation.question_text:
A connected network with $5$ vertices has a minimum spanning tree containing edges of weights $4, 6, 7$, and an unknown weight $k$.
If the total weight of the minimum spanning tree is $25$, calculate the value of $k$.
foundation.solution_text:
The total weight is the sum of all $n - 1 = 4$ edges in the MST.
$4 + 6 + 7 + k = 25$
$17 + k = 25$
$k = 25 - 17$
$= 8$

foundation.question_text:
A weighted graph with $4$ vertices has three candidate spanning trees:
Tree 1 has edges with weights $\{3, 4, 6\}$.
Tree 2 has edges with weights $\{2, 5, 6\}$.
Tree 3 has edges with weights $\{2, 4, 5\}$.
Determine which tree is the minimum spanning tree and state its total weight.
foundation.solution_text:
Calculate the total weight of each spanning tree:
$\text{Weight of Tree 1} = 3 + 4 + 6 = 13$
$\text{Weight of Tree 2} = 2 + 5 + 6 = 13$
$\text{Weight of Tree 3} = 2 + 4 + 5 = 11$
Tree 3 is the minimum spanning tree with a total weight of $11$.

foundation.question_text:
The distance table shows the edge weights of a connected network connecting four towns $A, B, C, D$.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{From/To} & A & B & C & D \\ \hline A & - & 5 & 8 & 3 \\ B & 5 & - & 4 & 6 \\ C & 8 & 4 & - & 7 \\ D & 3 & 6 & 7 & - \end{array}$
Construct the minimum spanning tree using Prim's algorithm and determine the total weight.

development.question_text:
A minimum spanning tree for a $6$-vertex network includes an edge with unknown weight $x$.
The known edge weights of the minimum spanning tree are $6, 8, 9$, and $12$.
If the total weight of the minimum spanning tree is $42$, calculate the value of $x$.
development.solution_text:
The MST of a $6$-vertex network has $6 - 1 = 5$ edges.
$\text{Sum of edges} = 6 + 8 + 9 + 12 + x$
$= 35 + x$
$35 + x = 42$
$x = 42 - 35$
$= 7$

development.question_text:
The table gives direct distances between five regional hubs $V, W, X, Y, Z$.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} \text{From/To} & V & W & X & Y & Z \\ \hline V & - & 6 & 9 & - & 4 \\ W & 6 & - & 5 & 8 & - \\ X & 9 & 5 & - & 3 & 7 \\ Y & - & 8 & 3 & - & 6 \\ Z & 4 & - & 7 & 6 & - \end{array}$
Apply Prim's algorithm starting at vertex $V$ to find the minimum spanning tree weight.

In a network, edges $AB$ of weight $5$ and $AC$ of weight $6$ are already part of a minimum spanning tree.
Explain why edge $BC$ of weight $4$ cannot be added to the tree, even though its weight is smaller than $AB$ and $AC$.
development.solution_text:
Vertices $B$ and $C$ are already connected in the tree via path $B\text{–}A\text{–}C$.
Adding edge $BC$ creates the closed cycle $A\text{–}B\text{–}C\text{–}A$.
A tree cannot contain cycles, so edge $BC$ cannot be added.

development.question_text:
A student proposes two spanning trees for a $5$-vertex weighted network:
Spanning Tree $A$ uses edges with weights $3, 5, 6, 8$.
Spanning Tree $B$ uses edges with weights $2, 4, 6, 7$.
Determine which spanning tree has the lower weight and find the difference in total weights.
development.solution_text:
$\text{Weight of Tree }A = 3 + 5 + 6 + 8 = 22$
$\text{Weight of Tree }B = 2 + 4 + 6 + 7 = 19$
$\text{Difference} = 22 - 19$
$= 3$
Spanning Tree $B$ has the lower total weight ($19$), which is $3$ units less than Tree $A$.

mastery.question_text:
A weighted network with $7$ vertices has a minimum spanning tree containing two unknown edge weights $a$ and $b$.
It is given that $a = b + 3$.
The known edge weights of the minimum spanning tree are $4, 6, 7$, and $9$.
If the total weight of the minimum spanning tree is $37$, calculate the values of $a$ and $b$.
In any connected weighted network with distinct edge weights, explain why the strictly heaviest edge in any cycle can never belong to a minimum spanning tree.
mastery.solution_text:
If spanning tree $T$ contains $e_{\max}$, removing $e_{\max}$ disconnects $T$ into two components.
Cycle $C$ contains another edge $e'$ connecting the components with $w(e') < w(e_{\max})$.
$w(T') = w(T) - w(e_{\max}) + w(e')$
$< w(T)$
Replacing $e_{\max}$ with $e'$ yields a spanning tree of strictly lower weight, so $e_{\max}$ cannot belong to an MST.
